A novel method is introduced to depict the Dunkl operator in one dimension, based on the classical reflection operator and the Laplace transformation. This approach enables a straightforward calculation of the Dunkl transformation and the associated $g$-function in any given order.

The galaxy NGC 5253, known for its starburst activity, is the subject of this study, which uses submillimeter observations to analyze its young stars. Our 12-meter ALMA data captures the H30$\alpha$ line, allowing us to pinpoint the locations of stars younger than 1 million years. Examinations reveal that young stars are concentrated in the northern half of NGC 5253, where the 100 Myr-old star cluster resides. Our analysis of the 1 million-year-old young stars indicates they are 10-20 kiloparsecs apart, with a higher density near the 100 Myr-old star cluster. The distribution of young stars is oriented along the direction of the galaxy's major axis. Our findings suggest that the formation of young stars in NGC 5253 is linked to the presence of the 100 Myr-old star cluster, with the metallicity of the galaxy influencing the formation of young stars.

Constant orbit equivalence stiffness, first introduced by Fabrykowski and Ozbaan in 2008, is the most stringent form of orbit equivalence between free actions of a group G on two spaces X and Y. In this study, we observe that the maximum observed orbit equivalence stiffness for virtually cyclic group actions on manifolds does not exceed square root of the order of the finite subgroup within the group. Through the use of this finding, we demonstrate that the three-sphere cannot be expressed as a quotient of a compact manifold by a virtually cyclic group with a non-trivial reduced Euler characteristic, and we also establish the constant orbit equivalence of free actions on manifolds by the group Zp times Zinfinity for the finite subgroup p in the order 6 and 10.

This chapter provides an overview of the Spline Regression Function estimation method, focusing on its underlying concepts and offering guidance for selecting optimal methods to estimate a regression function. It begins by defining the conditional expectation, which is the best possible estimator for a random variable y, given x, according to mean square error criteria. It then outlines the direct estimation method, which involves first estimating y and x, and subsequently calculating E(y | x) through the ratio of integrals. It also discusses the non-direct method, which involves estimating the joint probability density function and marginal density to find the conditional expectation.

Building upon the basic SIR epidemic model, this study develops an observer to estimate the dynamic states and employs a least-squares method to deduce model parameters based on a finite set of available data. In the observer design, the infection and recovery rates are formulated as non-negative functions of the model variables, with the least-squares method utilized to yield parameter estimates that ensure non-negative rates and thus, guaranteed observer stability. Theoretical analysis and simulation results are presented to substantiate the method's efficacy.

Prediction of temporal knowledge graph links involves forecasting the existence of relationships between entities in future time periods based on a historical knowledge graph. Current approaches for predicting links in temporal knowledge graphs often develop a model from scratch for each time period, which is computationally costly. To address this issue, we investigate methods for reusing a model across multiple time periods. To achieve this, we first need an approach for determining whether a model is suitable for a given time period. To tackle this challenge, we develop two methods: one analyzes entity and relationship representations to identify models that work well for specific instances, and another uses the quality of predictions on previously unseen data to evaluate the model. To determine the best model for a time period, we compare the quality of predictions across multiple models and select the one with the highest performance. To make the prediction process more efficient, we develop a data structure that allows for quick retrieval of the most relevant entity and relationship representations, reducing the computational cost of finding the best model. Experimental results using three different temporal knowledge graph datasets show that our approach significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods and achieves substantial query response time improvements.

Ultrashort pulse lasers with high-peak power can cause distortions in the laser beam. These pulses, affected by self-focusing, tend to have an uneven intensity profile, which in turn impacts the Kerr-lens mode-locking process. Research has shown that taking into account the distortions caused by the medium's nonlinearity is crucial for modeling this locking mechanism. Our study aims to analyze the geometric effects of these distortions on Kerr-lens mode-locking, with a focus on developing a new method for calculating the mode profile and stability diagram of the Kerr lens.

In the context of resource constraints, training a model efficiently becomes a significant challenge.  Asynchronous online learning offers a solution by processing data in real-time and utilizing resources sparingly. However, conventional asynchronous learning methods are limited by their reliance on linear models, making them unsuitable for complex tasks. Our contribution lies in developing a novel resource-conscious asynchronous model capable of performing nonlinear regression. Our approach combines a nonlinear regression technique, online matrix factorization and an adaptive learning rate mechanism to adjust model updates dynamically. Through theoretical and empirical analysis, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, which we validate through a comparison with standard models. Our results show that our novel asynchronous model can achieve performance comparable to its batch learning counterparts, while being more resource-efficient.

In the study, researchers developed a concept for a photonic crystal back reflector to enhance the absorption of light in very thin layers of silicon. They used a diamond lattice structure for the crystal, which exhibited a high level of absorption of light with a specific spectrum of around 400-1100 nanometers. By analyzing how this structure interacts with light, they discovered that certain orientations of the crystal could efficiently reflect most of the incident light. By incorporating a specific crystal layer, which was around 100 nanometers thick, into a device, the researchers were able to achieve a significant increase in the absorption of near-infrared light, which would otherwise be inefficiently absorbed. Furthermore, they found that thinner layers of silicon could also benefit from this technology, which could significantly reduce losses in near-infrared light.

This paper offers concise and direct proofs for the Riemann hypothesis equivalent assertion by Cayley and the alternative formulation proposed by Borwein, Borwein, and Girgensohn, in addition to finding the precise limit of the tetration formula's higher-order derivatives.

High dimensional expansions, such as high dimensional expansions of high order covers, offer a fresh perspective on analyzing stochastic systems. They are particularly useful in analyzing products of high dimensional random variables. A significant expansion, the Poisson-Wishart expansion, has been found to be a high dimensional expansion. In this study, we introduce a general framework for constructing high dimensional expansions from coverings of topological spaces. This approach allows us to create high dimensional expansions for a broader range of products, extending the applicability of this concept. Additionally, we derive a general bound for the total variation distance using high dimensional expansions and demonstrate their connection to coupling techniques. Furthermore, we explore the relationships between various expansion methods, including coupling, coupling from the past, and couplings from the distribution.

Our research focuses on investigating the magnetic properties of the hP9 structured compound GdInO$_3$, a quasi-two-dimensional centered honeycomb antiferromagnet. Bulk samples of this material were created and analyzed using various techniques including specific heat, magnetization, and zero field muon spin relaxation measurements. These experiments showed that GdInO$_3$ behaves as an antiferromagnet with an unusually low ordering temperature of 2.4 K, significantly lower than what is predicted by our initial analysis based on the Raman scattering data. Our zero field muon spin relaxation data further revealed that the ordering temperature of this material is actually around 2.4 K, indicating a possible effect of size on the ordering temperature. Our zero field muon spin relaxation data also showed that the ordering temperature of this material is independent of the applied magnetic field up to 7 T, indicating that the ordering temperature of this material is relatively high compared to other similar materials. These findings suggest that the magnetic interactions within this material are more complex than what is typically observed in other similar materials.

The task of link prediction involves forecasting connections between nodes in dynamic network environments, despite the absence of existing links between those nodes. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes sparse self-attention mechanisms to create comprehensive node representations, enabling the prediction of future links. To streamline computation and memory usage, we employ an efficient technique for merging identical nodes. The proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in speed and achieves higher accuracy across multiple large-scale network datasets.

Highly efficient optical access windows are crucial in nano-fabricated devices, particularly in those made of silicon. This window efficiency can be significantly enhanced by using a ruby-doped optical window. This window can be fabricated by growing a thin layer of solidified vapor that contains chromium atoms on a silicon substrate. The use of solid-state vapor deposition allows for the creation of a durable vapor layer that can withstand mechanical stress. The resulting chromium layer can then be transferred to the surface of a silicon substrate to create a ruby-doped optical window. The window can then be used to trap atomic atoms in the form of rubidium or cesium. The window can also be used to create a quantum memory in silicon. The window can also be used to create a quantum memory in silicon. The window can also be used to create a quantum memory in silicon.

This paper explores the DFTN power of dual-polarization 4D formats. We examine the DFTN power's characteristics in terms of the dual polarization's phase difference and investigate its implications for the DFTN power. We also analyze the DFTN power of specific dual polarization structures, such as Hadamard codes, random codes, and dual polarization with a phase shift of 90 degrees or 180 degrees. Our findings indicate that dual polarization structures with specific phase differences can achieve lower DFTN power, with Hadamard codes showing a difference in DFTN power of up to 2.5 dB compared to single polarization. We hope that our research will contribute to the development of dual polarization structures with optimal DFTN power.

Wildfire detection and early warning systems heavily rely on visual surveillance, but clear images are often hindered by low light and other visual obstructions. To address this issue, we've developed an innovative network, an end-to-end deep learning model that generates highly realistic, detailed fire images at a rapid pace. Unlike traditional image synthesis methods, our Fire Image Generation technique, an extension of the Relaxing Adversarial Inference in GANs method, directly optimizes image quality and other desired characteristics, resulting in more accurate and consistent fire images. By incorporating burning indicators and detailed texture analysis, our model produces highly realistic fire images that can significantly enhance wildfire management and surveillance systems.

A comprehensive dataset of social media posts from users exhibiting depression, along with related metadata, is presented. This dataset was compiled through an ongoing study exploring social media behavior in individuals suffering from depression. The dataset's quality is maintained by employing various filtering methods to eliminate spam, irrelevant content, and posts from non-depressed users. A total of approximately one million English posts from depression sufferers, spanning the period 2014-2019, are included. The study's data is accessible via https://github.com/ashokkumar1998/Social-Media-Data-Depression. Additionally, an empirical analysis is conducted to investigate the utility of social media as a tool for identifying early signs of depression, using the compiled dataset and comparing it to an external dataset. The study's results indicate that social media posts can effectively predict depression in both known and new users, highlighting its potential as an early warning system.

To create regional forecasts for COVID-19, a random SARS-CoV-2 compartmental model is developed, incorporating data from the Canadian Immunization Research Knowledge Network. This model accounts for uncertainties in key variables, including test positivity rates and vaccination rates. To our knowledge, a COVID-19 stochastic SEIR model with such integrated factors has not been explored in the existing literature. Our analysis reveals that vaccination efforts are the most effective means of reducing infections and deaths. Additionally, a significant increase in daily cases is expected if vaccination rates decline.

This work provides a comprehensive theoretical examination of the Isoscalar Giant Monopole Resonance (GMR) in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si, which are specific examples of vibrational nuclei. A newly developed version of the Energy Density Functional (EDF) in the time-domain, called the Time Dependent Variational Approach (TDHFB), is used in conjunction with a new method, the Backward-Forthward Correlated Ground State (BFGC), to calculate the properties of the GMR. Our $td$-HFB approach is complemented by the large scale Shell Model (LSM) calculations to study the GMR. Our results reveal that the GMR in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si exhibits a strong, collective nature, with frequencies that are in good agreement with the experimental data. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the GMR in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si is a combination of the Isoscalar Giant Monopole Resonance (GMR) and Isoscalar Giant Quadrupole Resonance (GQR), with the two resonances having a strong, mutual coupling.

This paper examines the stability of systems governed by Coulomb friction through feedback control. A mathematical model developed for these systems captures the dynamic behavior of frictional interfaces and their friction coefficient changes over time. To ensure system stability, friction control is applied to adjust the coefficient based on a convergence-stable criterion. Computational analysis of models with dynamic system components and a convergence criterion shows that various parameters influence the emergence of stick-slip and convergence phenomena. Notably, systems exhibiting both splay and convergence friction coefficient changes are also studied.

This paper introduces the concept of Bellman risk management, which involves optimizing a combination of the expected return and a function of uncertain reward distributions-critical for tackling issues such as distribution shifts and model robustness. To address these challenges, this study proposes the Bellman risk propagation operator, a method for computing higher-order risk moments of the expected return in model-based reinforcement learning scenarios. Focusing on higher-order Gaussian approximations, this research derives Gaussian Bellman propagation operators and evaluates the effectiveness of this approach in a series of mathematical and experimental evaluations.

Sequential recommender systems, which rely heavily on historical item interactions, often overlook the essential aspect of user interest in specific items. A new framework called HUI is introduced to address this limitation, focusing on a latent variable that represents user interest in specific items. HUI is used to enhance the performance of sequential recommender systems by integrating it with their training process. To validate the effectiveness of HUI, it is integrated into the sequential recommender system T5, and the modified version is tested using a semi-supervised training approach on a widely used public dataset called Amazon Reviews2018. Evaluation results show that adding the HUI component to T5 leads to improved performance across multiple metrics.

The solvable double confluent Heun equation is analyzed in detail, leading to a comprehensive method for solving it. This involves establishing a connection between the equation and its formal solutions, which are also found to be generalized forms of the solvable outset. A formal solution to the equation is shown to be expressible as a linear combination of the known outset solutions, with the establishment of specific conditions. Ultimately, the connection between the double confluent Heun equation and the solvable outset provides an interesting insight into the underlying structure of the equation.

Matrix analysis is a crucial component of many data-driven fields, with numerous applications.  However, several data-driven processes are currently based on a case-by-case basis, with no clear understanding of the underlying theoretical frameworks.  In response, this study aims to investigate the theoretical underpinnings of a particular process, a variant of low-rank matrix evaluation with partitioning, which is widely used to tackle issues of heterogeneity.  The proposed research focuses on analyzing the proposed model, which involves both group-wise differences and noise.  By applying the tools of statistical physics, we derive a condition for phase transition and provide an analytical expression for a rank-one estimator, which is applicable to the entire set of constraints.  Additionally, we show that the model exhibits two distinct states, with spin-glass and paramagnetic solutions, which have been observed in similar research.  In order to verify the validity of the results, numerical simulations are conducted.  Interestingly, the model reveals that a particular threshold, which is referred to as the saturation threshold, must be reached to achieve the optimal low-rank solution.  Furthermore, the model also reveals that a particular condition must be satisfied to achieve this threshold, which is characterized by an interplay between the model's parameters.

Quantum systems displaying symmetry-protected topological order can be distinguished by their ability to be split into separate sections, each characterized by an integer value. When symmetry is broken, our research reveals that certain topological properties retain themselves in any possible configuration. To establish this, we demonstrate that a particular Hamiltonian, which incorporates local operations, represents a system inherently possessing an extra dimension. The preserved topological characteristics in the original system are linked to this inherent dimensionality. The findings are validated through numerical simulations of a spin model on the honeycomb lattice, which exhibits robust symmetry protection when the symmetry is weakened.

The semi-inclusive Lepton Flavor Equivalence ratio, a parameter that compares semi-leptonic differential cross-sections with different neutral current types, is a valuable tool for investigating new physics beyond the standard model. This parameter, which can be measured in the laboratory, is less susceptible to theoretical uncertainties related to hadronic matrix elements. Current measurements from the LHCb and ATLAS experiments agree with the standard model predictions. A detailed study of the standard model predictions, including precise calculations of the hadronic contribution and estimates of the systematic error, has been conducted. The hadronic contribution was calculated using the same set of form factors for the $B\to K^{(*)}$ and $B\to J/\psi$ transitions, leading to a theoretically robust prediction with minimal uncertainty. The standard model prediction for the ratio, which includes a precise calculation of the lepton kinematics factor and an estimate of the experimental bias, is $1.002\pm 0.004$. The precision of this parameter is expected to improve with the increased data samples at the LHCb Factory.

This paper presents a new approach to achieving coordination in complex network systems. A novel architecture is proposed, allowing for the flexible distribution of a distributed control strategy across a linear system with multiple inputs and outputs. The strategy employs a centralized calculation module, which can be placed at any node, and observer-based control rules at each individual system component. A key advantage of this approach is its ability to maintain stability and a specific calculation structure regardless of the communication network topology, as long as the module is positioned strategically. A 'calculator placement' concept is introduced, allowing for an optimal distribution of the control module to ensure observability. Numerical examples demonstrate the practical benefits of this approach, showcasing its ability to reduce communication overhead, improve computational efficiency, and enhance robustness against network disruptions. The results show that the proposed architecture can lead to more efficient and reliable control performance, even when using simple topologies like star networks, and with minimal computational resources required at each individual system component.

The COVID-19 outbreak is a major global event that has caused significant loss of life and severe economic disruption.  To better understand the disease, researchers have focused on categorizing patients into two groups, healthy and sick, based on their X-ray images.  However, using deep learning techniques to automatically classify COVID-19 patients based on these images remains a challenging task.  To overcome this challenge, researchers have developed an improved version of BERT, known as BERT-A, which incorporates the unique characteristics of COVID-19 X-ray images.  BERT-A uses image attributes to classify images and improve the classification process.  To further optimize the model, researchers have designed an efficient search algorithm that identifies the most important images for classification.  To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, researchers have tested it on a dataset of 1,000 COVID-19 X-ray images and compared it to other COVID-19 classification models.

This article is a comprehensive review of fundamental research on network analysis, covering its core principles and methodologies. It serves as an entry point for those interested in network research, particularly those with a background in optimization, ODEs, probability, and statistics. Initially, the article delves into the fundamental concepts of characterizing and estimating network structures and processes, including network inference, reconstruction, and parameter estimation. Subsequently, it explores the application of network models to solve practical problems. Key topics within this article encompass network topologies, dynamic network behavior, network clustering, community detection, and various network-based tasks such as node classification, link prediction, and graph simulation.

The development of living organisms is a complex process that spans ancient times to the present day.
This study investigates the ecological and evolutionary connections and their shifts in time, focusing on the co-occurrence of species and the exchange of genetic traits.
By using a new method of quantitative analysis, the research aims to uncover the causes and mechanisms behind these changes, specifically the duration of interactions and the factors influencing their rates.
This approach is applied to the study of evolutionary transitions in social behaviors, examining the impact of ecological and evolutionary factors on changes in ecological networks and genetic traits over time.
The analysis reveals that the duration of species interactions and the factors influencing genetic trait exchanges have played significant roles in the evolution of social behaviors, with the emergence of new traits and the modification of ecological networks being driven by both ecological and evolutionary factors.
This study's findings provide valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying the ecological and evolutionary connections and their changes in time, with the potential to inform our understanding of the evolution of living organisms and the ecological systems they inhabit.

Current speech research has largely overlooked the possibility that speech self-supervised models, trained on unlabelled data, might inadvertently cause downstream models to learn harmful biases or representations. To address this potential issue, a comprehensive study was conducted, which involved creating alternative evaluation methods to identify and measure these hidden biases. By combining new evaluation techniques with ablation experiments, researchers were able to thoroughly investigate the existence and characteristics of these hidden biases. Furthermore, the study examined the underlying reasons for these biases and proposed potential solutions to mitigate them.

This study examines the potential of blockchain technology to enhance distributed trade-on platforms. The findings indicate that the integration of blockchain can fill a significant gap in the literature, offering an innovative platform for managing distributed exchanges. The research illustrates how blockchain can address key challenges in trade process automation, system reliability, and security. The study highlights the benefits of blockchain, including its scalability, traceability, and resistance to tampering, which contribute to the transparency, immutability, and trustworthiness of trade records. The use of smart contracts enables a seamless and transparent trade process, eliminating the need for intermediaries and reducing transaction costs. The transparency of blockchain also allows for real-time monitoring and analysis of trade data, enabling stakeholders to make informed decisions and fostering accountability. The outcomes of this research have the potential to provide valuable insights into the operationalization of trade processes and the implementation of distributed systems.

Epidemiologists' conclusions about disease risk factor associations are frequently influenced by biases in existing research. To address this, researchers utilize diverse statistical methods to gauge the magnitude of bias in their findings. A crucial type of bias in meta-analyses and large-scale studies arises from studies with missing individual-level data. A recent study in the American Statistical Association's journal proposed the E-value, a metric to assess robustness in observational studies, but it has limitations when applied to datasets with absent information. This study expands on the E-value concept, presenting a method to perform sensitivity analyses on datasets with missing individuals, taking into account uncertainty. To achieve this, we utilize a Bayesian latent missingness model to estimate the proportion of missing studies supporting our null and alternative hypotheses. To account for uncertainty, we employ the total-evidence approach, integrating all available data into our analysis. Our method's performance is demonstrated through two empirical applications: a case-control study examining statin use and Alzheimer's disease, and a large-scale study of socioeconomic status and Alzheimer's disease in the UK Biobank.

This study explores how modified quantum sl2 operators interact with a specific algebraic structure, denoted as $\mathbb{C}\left\langle x,y,z,w\right\rangle$, which is defined by two key relationships: $yw-wy=q^2$ and $qw-wq=q^{-2}$. The remaining variables $x$ and $z$ commute with each other and $y$, while differing only in their interaction with $w$ and $q$. We've identified and categorized all possible symmetries within this framework that adhere to the sl2 relationship, discovering that they can be categorized into distinct groups based on their characteristics.

The ever-evolving Internet of Vehicles (IoV) has significantly transformed the way drivers and passengers interact, enabling seamless communication and data exchange between vehicles and infrastructure.  However, the development of trusted education systems for drivers and passengers has been a significant challenge.  Recent research has focused on creating secure and reliable education platforms using technology such as federated learning and blockchain.  Despite the growing interest, there is a lack of comprehensive studies on this topic.  This study aims to fill this knowledge gap by examining the existing literature and evaluating the advantages and limitations of blockchain-enabled federated education systems within the context of IoV.  By leveraging technology-based approaches, this research seeks to enhance the understanding of stakeholders and pave the way for future studies and applications.

The production of open charm quarks in high-energy proton-proton collisions at a high energy of 5.02 TeV has been studied using the LHCb detector. Measurements were taken in two distinct rapidity ranges and two distinct transverse momentum ranges. Both the non-prompt and direct D mesons were used to derive nuclear modification factors, which were found to decrease with increasing transverse momentum. This decrease in nuclear modification factor is attributed to energy loss experienced by fast partons as they travel through the quark-gluon plasma.

The burgeoning field of quantum computing is experiencing rapid growth, with notable advancements being made by tech giants such as IBM, Google, and Rigetti Computing, who have developed and tested small-scale quantum processors up to 65 qubits. To facilitate the continued development of quantum computing at Fermilab's Main Laboratory Complex, we have constructed a $1.2 million dilution refrigerator with a millikelvin platform, capable of supporting up to 100 high-performance D-Wave style superconducting qubits. This facility, located at a site with abundant electrical power and low electromagnetic interference, is ideally situated to support quantum computing research and is available to external users for testing and experimenting with quantum processors.

Cryptocurrency technology has the potential to significantly transform the financial industry, offering enhanced security and efficiency. However, the development of dApps and smart contracts is hindered by the lack of expertise and the high costs associated with it. To address this issue, some tools and platforms have been developed to assist developers, including Python frameworks for building dApps and smart contracts, and analyzing blockchain data. This paper examines how Python is used within the blockchain ecosystem by investigating 1,586 GitHub repositories, resulting in the identification of 41 common Python-related misuses. These misuses are categorized into seven groups, including 'not suitable for blockchain,' 'not open to public scrutiny,' 'not well-documented,' 'not thoroughly tested,' 'not properly maintained,' 'not well-optimized,' and 'not open source.' Furthermore, the paper provides a detailed analysis of Python misuse in PyChain, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed classification system.

Automatically labeling people in videos or images based on their appearance is
a crucial step in visual analysis, but it remains underutilized in current
computer vision research. Most existing methods rely on either manual surveys or
automated methods with limited scope, focusing on specific domains. This study
introduces a comprehensive, multi-domain dataset, featuring people's appearances
from various categories, and relies on a massive-scale, crowd-sourced approach
for automatic tagging by analyzing the movements of people in public spaces.
This new approach, which involves analyzing the movements of people in public
spaces, enables the creation of a large, diverse database of automatic labels
covering 800 categories, and demonstrates the effectiveness of the method by
showing that it can be used to improve performance on related tasks, such as
image classification and object detection.

A new optimization model for the seismic reflectivity recovery model has been proposed, where the reflectivity is represented as a collection of sparse components located at arbitrary positions with varying amplitudes, allowing for a more accurate representation of non-uniformly distributed geological features. To achieve this, a proximal mean network has been developed, effectively approximating the l0 norm of these components, and further regularized using a prior distribution. The resulting optimization model has been tested and demonstrated superior performance when compared to the traditional l2 regularization, particularly on real-world data.

Our investigation centers on the link between integral operators and semigroups of composition operators that act within function spaces characterized by BMOA-like properties. Specifically, we establish a criterion for the boundedness of $K_{\phi}$ in the context of $BMO_{\Gamma,\mu}^{p}$ with $\|\frac{\overline{\varphi^{\prime}(z)}}{(1-\varphi(z)^{2})}\|_{L^{p}(\mu)}<\infty$, for all $p>0$. Furthermore, under certain conditions, including $\mu$ being the area measure and $\varphi(z)=\lambda z$, the operators $K_{\phi}$ are shown to be compact in $BMO_{\Gamma,\mu}^{p}$ for $0<p<\infty$.

We examine the behavior of the finite-size corrections in the free-energy of the Haagerup model near its critical point. By employing a combination of conformal field theory and matrix product state methods, our findings reveal that the corrections are model-specific but can be predicted for various one-dimensional quantum systems. These corrections are shown to be directly related to the ground-state overlap between corresponding conformal field theory wavefunctions, offering a streamlined approach for evaluating finite-size effects. Our numerical results demonstrate a length-scale exponent of approximately 0.4, in addition to specific coefficients for each relevant primary field. These specific coefficients enable the determination of the critical free-energy with enhanced precision, surpassing what can be achieved by extrapolating from critical point calculations.

Historical documents, encompassing diary entries, letters, and other personal writings, hold significant value for researchers studying historical contexts, social dynamics, and linguistic evolution. However, accessing these documents in full text is often hindered by their unprocessed, annotated, or unknown origins. Developing tools to analyze such documents is crucial, particularly for determining their Part-of-Speech (POS) structure. Existing tools are insufficient for documents lacking processing, so we suggest using Part-of-Speech Forecasting (POSF) as a new approach to handle the uncertainty of unconstrained documents. POSF predicts the potential distribution of POS tags for each word in a given document. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on 19th-century English letters from the University of Texas at Austin, showcasing its ability to provide more accurate and informative results compared to traditional single-valued forecasting methods.

This article focuses on extending fractal footprint integrality conditions to functions with non-smooth solutions to dynamic systems governed by non-empty, bounded, and frame-subordinate control sets, where the driving function and vector fields are only hypo-graphic in terms of smoothness. Key to this framework is the use of sub-densities and upper densities to establish integrality conditions, which are shown to be equivalent through sub-density/upper density pairs. This study builds upon previous work, where similar principles were established for smooth functions and control sets, to provide a more comprehensive and flexible framework.

A crucial step in developing safety-critical software systems is translating a city's requirements into formal specifications.  Current methods are inefficient, often relying on time-consuming and error-prone manual processes.  To address this issue, we propose an innovative approach that enables a city resident to input their safety-related expectations in everyday language, which a knowledge-based system then translates into formal specifications.  By utilizing ontologies and natural language processing, our method accurately converts safety-critical requirements from unstructured text into structured formal declarations.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through integration with the REVAS platform, which allows for the automatic generation of test cases based on the generated formal specifications.

In the quantum error correction process, it's essential to apply inverse operations to cancel out errors. However, implementing these inverse operations is a complex task, especially when using superconducting quantum devices. A major obstacle is that certain operations, like Pauli X, have inverse operations that are the same, while others, like S, are self-inversing, leading to identical phases when applied. This problem is compounded by the presence of noise, which can cause phase errors during quantum computations. To overcome this issue, we have developed a new method to conceal the inverse operations and mitigate the effects of phase errors. We have demonstrated this method using IBM's quantum device and successfully applied it to reduce errors in the teleportation of an arbitrary qubit.

In an extensive category with power objects, any preorder can be represented as a subobject in the category of subobjects of the terminal object. A key factor is the ability to depict the order relationship between subobjects as a preorder, specifically through cocartesian connections. A category meeting these criteria is referred to as an extensive category with depictions. An equivalence connection is a special type of discrete relation, and a category can represent the relationship between subobjects through equivalence connections, specifically through depictions. An equivalence of categories can be represented as a special type of connection, and a category can represent this relationship through depictions, specifically through connections that satisfy certain conditions. An important result states that if a category represents equivalence of categories through depictions, then it also satisfies extensivity. Another important result states that if a category satisfies extensivity and certain other conditions, then it represents an equivalence of categories if and only if a certain equivalence of connections represents an isomorphism.

To better prepare for extreme tides, wind, and water levels in marine settings, 
spatial models are used to analyze and simulate these environments jointly.
A new statistical model has been developed to predict the simultaneous 
extremes in these environments based on observed data from multiple locations.
This model is based on the Extremal Coefficient Function and the Gaussian copula, 
allowing it to estimate probability thresholds for complex events to occur.
The model has been tested using data from the UK and is capable of accurately 
predicting the joint extremes in three environments at multiple locations.
The model's ability to accurately forecast these complex events is crucial for 
assessing the risk of damage to infrastructure and marine facilities.

State-of-the-art vision-language models like CLIP and ViT-B/16-CLIP excel at visual understanding but are limited by their reliance on a single training image per image-text pair. To address this issue, we utilize a vocabulary-based language model to generate detailed, multi-sentence descriptions for each training image. These descriptive texts are then used to fine-tune the ViT-B/16-CLIP model, significantly enhancing its zero-shot performance on various downstream tasks. Moreover, our generated texts demonstrate a high level of accuracy and clarity, surpassing that of models like BEiT and BLIP.

We have developed an efficient and versatile approach for rapidly simulating a matrix-coefficient matrix differential equation. Our method employs a continuous piecewise-constant approximation where each segment is represented by the eigendecomposition of the matrix, allowing us to analytically determine the time-evolution operator. By strategically selecting intervals, we can control the approximation error. To achieve this, we formulate an eigenvalue-based error bound criterion and use it to iteratively adjust the step size. Our approach is exemplified by its application to modeling operator switching under noisy conditions.

We identify the $k$-th homotopy group of the $K(K(\mathbb{H}^p; \mathbb{H}^q), k)$ after $K(\mathbb{H}^q; k)$- localization in terms of $k$, $p$, $q$, and calculate the homotopy groups of the Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectrum $Y = K(\mathbb{H}^2; 2)$ after $K(K(\mathbb{H}^2; 2))$- localization.

This text discusses a text version of a 2018 publication, and the author's 2018 publication, "Compact Hilbert Ring Operators and Adjoint Ideals" (Adv. Stud. Contemp. Math., Kem. Bridge Press), should not be confused for this one. The text begins with an introduction to a new compact operator that generalizes F-adjoint ideals to rings that are not necessarily complete. The definition of this operator and its properties are then explored, and the operator is shown to be equal to zero in certain cases, such as a specific type of ring. The operator is also shown to be continuous and related to a notion of depth, and its values are non-zero only up to a certain dimension. The operator is further shown to be closely related to test elements and is used to identify certain types of rings. The author also explores the connections between these operators and other notions of ring classification, such as regularity and F-regularity.

The application of machine learning in medical imaging has yielded promising results for diagnostics, but several obstacles hinder its practical implementation. One significant issue is the lack of unified standards for organizing datasets, training procedures, and outcome reporting. This has led to difficulties in replicating and validating findings. To address this challenge, a Python-based library, Highdicom, has been developed to facilitate the exchange of high-resolution medical imaging data, machine learning model development, and performance reporting in a cohesive manner. This paper outlines the rationale behind Highdicom's design, demonstrates its usage through a step-by-step tutorial, and showcases its benefits with a detailed case study.

A detailed analysis of the Einstein-Hilbert action's boundary terms is conducted, resulting in a novel expression for the Noether charge two-form. This boundary expression is derived directly, in contrast to conventional approaches, and a generalized approach to BMS algebra is developed. By applying the generalized Noether charge method, specifically the Abbott-Deser-Robinson method, the standard Virahoro algebra and the Brown-Henneaux central charge are reproduced. Furthermore, the radial evolution of the Noether charge two-form is examined, leading to the derivation of the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy for a black hole.

In recent years, DNA sequence analysis has gained significant attention due to its diverse applications in various fields, including the identification of similar sequences, predicting functionally significant features, and detecting patterns within sequences. Our research focuses on developing an unsupervised method for learning DNA sequence embeddings without the need for labeled data. By applying a novel training technique that uses a combination of n-gram matching and random walk objectives, we are able to generate embeddings that capture the similarities between DNA sequences. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through its superior performance in a clustering task, where it produces more accurate results compared to other methods, including word2vec and fastText. Furthermore, we find that our embeddings can also be used for the purpose of classification, thus facilitating further analysis of DNA sequences.

The interaction at the interface between metallic layers and insulating layers is crucial in various applications including magnetic storage, power transmission, and advanced nanotechnology. In particular, the interaction between the layers can induce the V ions in the insulating V$_2$O$_3$ film to become more metallic when in contact with an Ir metal. In order to understand this interaction, researchers studied the interaction between the metallic layers and the insulating layers by controlling the thickness of the metallic layers and observed the effect of the metallic layers on the insulating layers. By not having a buffer layer between the metallic layers and the insulating layers, researchers observed the interaction between the metallic layers and the insulating layers to be stronger and caused the insulating layers to become more metallic. In contrast, researchers observed the interaction between the metallic layers and the insulating layers to be weaker when having a buffer layer of MgO between the metallic layers and the insulating layers. These results suggest that the interaction between the metallic layers and the insulating layers can be controlled by controlling the thickness of the metallic layers and by introducing a buffer layer between the metallic layers and the insulating layers.

The Clebsch variable technique for reducing the Euler-Poisson dynamics has been generalized within the Lie-Poisson structure, resulting in the development of a novel conjugation method for Lie-algebraic systems. This concept is applied to Euler fluids and the Chern-Simons theory, leading to the derivation of Eulerian energy minimization principles. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the current conjugates are constrained to specific submanifolds, which explains the origin of Noether charges associated with symmetry groups.

Our goal is to identify and analyze exoplanets detected by the KMTNet microlensing survey, specifically those that exhibit a characteristic short time lag between the primary and secondary lensing events. In 2018, a total of 23 planets outside the Hubble Space Telescope's prime field were identified, with the majority of them located in the Cygnus and Orion regions. The detected planets have mass ratios ranging from approximately 0.0001 to 0.004, with the majority of them having inclination angles similar to those observed in the Solar System, according to statistical analysis. Furthermore, a significant discrepancy was found between the mass ratios of the planets detected by KMTNet and those detected by other studies, indicating a discrepancy in the distribution of planets in the sub-prime field. Additionally, the distribution of planets in the sub-prime field is found to be consistent with the overall distribution of planets in the Milky Way galaxy, indicating that the detected planets are representative of the overall population.

A novel method for creating accurate numerical algorithms is introduced, enabling the precise pressure-velocity coupling in both compressible and incompressible flows. These algorithms maintain key physical principles such as mass, momentum, and energy conservation across a range of applications from low to high Mach numbers. Moreover, they pose no issues related to stability at low Mach numbers. As a result, these algorithms provide a reliable and versatile framework for solving a wide variety of flow problems. A comprehensive overview of a specific finite volume method implementation is presented, which maintains the accurate representation of physical conservation principles at both the algorithmic and discrete levels. This approach was successfully applied to model various phenomena, including shock waves, natural and forced instabilities, and fluid-structure interactions. A detailed description of the algorithmic principles and the results of the application are presented, along with the associated numerical outcomes.

The National Physical Laboratory's electron counting innovation has significantly boosted our understanding of electron nature and has also made a substantial impact in advancing digital technology.  Due to the widespread application of electron sources, there is a substantial amount of data generated daily.  To identify patterns in this data, there is a pressing need for efficient feature selection and pattern recognition methods.  This research focuses on developing machine learning-based algorithms to analyze Non-Photonic Counting (NPL) data.  Firstly, we employed different feature selection techniques to identify significant features, and subsequently, we assessed the performance of multiple machine learning algorithms on the (NPL) dataset.  Experimental results indicate that the Random Forest algorithm achieved the highest accuracy of 90% and achieved significant feature relevance using the mRMR technique.

A square board, denoted as $B_n$, is referred to as the Aztec Order $n$ board, where $n$ represents a positive integer. We are only considering placements of non-attacking rooks on this board. The set of all such valid placements for $n$ is denoted as $\mathcal{D}_n$. Our approach involves developing a multivariate generating function, $\mathcal{Z}_n(\mathbf{x})$, where each element in $\mathcal{D}_n$ contributes a specific term, based on the heights of the respective Dyck paths. The resulting function can be expressed as the sum of the elementary symmetric functions, $\mathcal{E}_n(t, q) = \sum_{r=0}^n e_{r} (t, q) t^{r}$.

Deep learning-based convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved exceptional performance in various visual tasks, primarily due to their ability to automatically learn from data. However, their high computational requirements and complex training process pose significant challenges. This study presents an innovative, modular CNN design, which is lightweight and efficient, and features a simplified structure that facilitates parameter reduction while maintaining performance. By incorporating rotational symmetry and employing group convolution, the proposed architecture reduces model complexity and memory usage, and enables the model to learn orientation-invariant representations. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that pre-training with oriented data and using transfer learning can yield even better results. Experimental results on benchmark datasets validate the efficacy of the proposed modulated CNN and offer a promising solution for various visual tasks.

A recent investigation by the second author and F. M. Goodman focused on specific subsets within the unit interval that remain unchanged when applying Laplacian transformations to subinterval linear mappings. Building upon this work, we now consider a more complex scenario involving a collection of subinterval linear mappings within the unit circle, where the curved segments possess a negative constant Gaussian curvature. In this context, we have developed a novel relative trace equation that enables the calculation of the Gaussian curvature of an invariant measure for a Gaussian band Laplacian, provided the invariant measure is known for one of the Laplacian mappings. This equation is utilized to determine the entropy of the invariant measure for the Gaussian band Laplacian, with the entropy being a function of the rotation angle. Additionally, the dependence of the invariant measure on the rotation angle is examined for the Gaussian band Laplacian, with the case of no flux being analyzed in detail.

We have developed an approximate, flavor-dependent top quark weight operator within substantial QCD frameworks that effectively captures the substantial flavor-dependent top quark dependence. This operator exhibits explicit weights for each flavor and is not sensitive to nonperturbative QCD effects. It can be utilized to enhance the accuracy of top quark matrix element calculations in high-energy processes involving top quark production and decay. This research provides an in-depth investigation into substantial flavor-dependent top quark effects, which could be crucial for precise calculations in high-energy physics.

Our findings demonstrate that, for a specified maximum degree of at most half the graph's number of vertices minus a constant, any sufficiently large graph with a minimum degree of at least half the graph's number of vertices plus a significant fraction times its square root can be colored in a particular way. Specifically, for any positive values of k and r, an edge coloring exists in which every subgraph with no more than k vertices is also edge colored with no more than r colors. This can be achieved by randomly assigning colors to the edges.

We establish a broad set of contraction inequalities for weighted $L^2$ spaces on the unit disk, where functions are orthogonal polynomials of bounded degree, leveraging an understanding of the Bergman kernel's behavior near the boundary.

A global pandemic has been caused by the novel coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), which is spreading rapidly and causing significant loss of life. A critical factor in controlling the spread of COVID-19 is early and accurate detection, which can be achieved through a lung CT scan. However, radiation exposure from high-dose CT scans is a serious concern, prompting the need for an effective way to analyze low-dose CT scans. A proposed framework involves a time-distributed capsule network, which is initially trained on low-dose data and then refined using full-dose medical images. This model, when applied to a benchmark dataset, demonstrated superior performance compared to other top-performing systems.

This study investigates the orbital capacity of low-Earth orbit by examining the ZEM-ZEO orbital formation method, which enables multiple spacecraft to maintain a stable geometric configuration through mutual gravitational interaction. By analyzing two- and multi-spacecraft formations, this research determines the maximum number of spacecraft that can be deployed in various orbital arrangements, including equatorial and inclined orbits, while maintaining specific geometric configurations. To achieve this, a geometric model is developed that maps out allowable regions for spacecraft deployment, considering factors such as stationkeeping, fuel consumption, and collision risk. Additionally, this study incorporates constraints related to solar panel dimensions to provide a more realistic analysis. The results of this research have significant implications for future space missions, including the deployment of large constellations and mega-constellations.

Creating unstructured high-quality 2D meshes on 3D models involves a crucial step where quadrilateral elements must be mapped onto the model. To achieve this, we propose an innovative linear optimization approach that takes input from Designation Meshes, which specify desired mesh sizes on the model. Our method employs two key strategies: first, we use line sweeping to organize mesh vertices along internal lines; second, we apply a number-based approach to align these vertices. By leveraging these techniques, we can generate high-order 2D meshes directly from user-defined mesh sizes, eliminating the need for intermediate, pre-processed data. Our approach has been successfully tested on various complex models, including those with curved surfaces and internal cavities, resulting in high-quality 2D meshes that accurately capture the model's geometry.

Permutational tests, also known as randomization tests, exchange random arrangements of observed data to create an exact analytical null distribution without relying on theoretical assumptions. This paper aims to create analytical formulas for the first four moments of the sample correlation variable under various random arrangements of the data samples, and we also provide a brief overview of the null distributions for the t-statistic and F-statistic in hypothesis testing for sample correlation by using the derived results for sample correlation moments. The derived moments and their corresponding numerical values can be utilized in various permutation-based statistical inference procedures. Furthermore, the moment formulas for sample correlation are applicable to other types of sample statistical tests, and the underlying logic can be extended to other tests, and the paper includes a comprehensive proof for these underlying results.

This review outlines the application of the S-matrix approach to scattering amplitudes in the context of scalar fields and black holes in both classical general relativity and quantum field theories. It delves into scalar solitons, black holes, and the gravitational scattering of both point particles and extended objects like strings and supergravity. A key aspect explored is the connection between low-energy gravity and the principles of effective field theory, as well as an examination of generalizations to higher-dimensional and non-commutative spaces. Additionally, the review discusses scalar solitons, black holes, and the scattering of higher-spin particles and objects, with an emphasis on implications for quantum gravity and string theory.

This study proposes a universal stabilization approach for solutions governed by three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations over a bounded domain with smooth edges. By utilizing a finite dimensional, location-specific and state-dependent algorithmic method, we effectively stabilize the system in various critical Sobolev and Besov spaces through reverse integration of an approximate inverse system. The obtained results span across the entire critical spectrum and encompass the most demanding space $H^{1/2}(\Omega)$, in addition to less demanding spaces such as $\dot{H}^{1-\varepsilon}(\Omega)$ and $\dot{B}_{2,2}^{1-\varepsilon}(\Omega)$.

Language learning through dictionary usage is widely prevalent, yet creating comprehensive dictionaries for less commonly studied languages poses significant challenges. As a remedy, this research introduces LitMind, a dictionary-based web platform designed to accelerate language learning for Indonesian users. Unlike conventional dictionaries, LitMind incorporates innovative lexicographical elements such as synonyms, antonyms, idioms, and word collocations, thereby providing a more comprehensive lexical understanding. Furthermore, LitMind is customizable to cater to diverse learner needs and can be easily adapted to other languages. The project's source code and database are publicly available, presenting a novel open-source collaboration initiative in language technology.

Recent developments in explainable AI have sparked interest in offering interpretable insights into AI-driven recommendations. A promising approach, LIME, has been adapted for this purpose, employing counterfactual data to generate local explanations for specific user-item interactions. However, current LIME RS explanations are limited to single factors affecting recommendations, which may not accurately reflect how multiple factors interact to influence user preferences. Moreover, it has not been established that such explanations can be reliably reproduced. This paper introduces a novel LIME RS variant that considers only the top item being explained, ensuring compliance with the ranking of all other items, and addresses the issue of reproducibility by addressing a key concern in LIME RS interpretations.

The behavior of the Fermi level in type-II quantum wells is not well understood, 
which poses significant challenges for the development of efficient infrared devices.
Our study focuses on a specific system, namely InAs quantum wells grown on GaInAs
substrates, where the Fermi level tends to become 'stuck' at the barrier material's 
band edge due to interfacial states. This issue can be resolved by incorporating a
thin Ga cap layer on the quantum well's surface, which effectively mitigates the 
undesirable surface states that typically contribute to barrier states' occupation.
Moreover, we discovered that barrier states are only significantly occupied when the 
barrier thickness exceeds a certain threshold of 3 nm, whereas the fundamental
electron and heavy hole states remain populated in thinner barriers.

In decentralized machine learning, when multiple agents share data across devices, they work together to train a model through multiple steps of computation. This collaborative approach is particularly useful when dealing with data that follows a non-uniform distribution, known as data heterogeneity, by aggregating models from different regions to mitigate the issue. However, when the boundaries between these different data distributions are unclear, the benefit of regional aggregation is unclear. Our research aims to clarify this by investigating the conditions under which regional aggregation is beneficial in heterogeneous data environments. We have developed a new analytical framework that models the differences between data distributions using various metrics. This framework allows us to determine when regional aggregation outperforms other approaches, providing both theoretical and practical insights. Our experiments across multiple machine learning problems confirm the validity of our findings.

We introduce a precise and efficient method for calculating the optimal transport matrix $W$ between two discrete probability distributions with $n$ support points each, requiring linear time complexity. This is made possible by the existence of a triangular array of probability distributions with the sinkhorn parameter $\sigma$ as a function of the support size $n$ and the array indices, where $\sigma$ is linear. The optimal transport matrix $W$ between distributions with $n$ and $n+1$ support points remains invariant and can be represented as $e^{\theta}a_n(a_n+a_{n+1})^{-1}$ for some $n$-dependent parameter $\theta$. The underlying probability distributions form a triangular array with rich properties. We prove that a particular subsequence of this array converges to a normal distribution and analyze other asymptotic properties. We also show that certain subarrays converge to a Gaussian field. We discover that $W$ between any two distributions within the triangular array is bi-stochastic and exhibits a non-trivial pattern. We identify explicit connections between this triangular array and the hypergeometric distribution, providing new insights into the hypergeometric distribution. We demonstrate that the hypergeometric distribution can be embedded within certain subarrays of the triangular array, yielding precise and efficient computations of optimal transport costs. The young star AU Mic is known for its variability and FUV emission, which significantly affects the evolution of planets within its habitable zone, including AU Mic b and c. A study on the connection between FUV variability and stellar activity in AU Mic, including quiescent and eruptive phases, reveals that the star's FUV emission in dormancy and during eruptions is primarily composed of the hot FUV component, with the latter lasting 2-3 days. FUV emissions during dormancy are linked to the star's activity, as seen in H-alpha and H-alpha in quiescence. The peak FUV emission levels during eruptions are 2-3 times higher than during dormancy. The duration of the hot component's rise and fall during eruptions is similar, and the energy released during these eruptions is comparable to the energy needed to impact the atmospheres of AU Mic b and c. The findings suggest that the evolution of the cool component's behavior during repeated eruptions may influence the evolution of the planets, and further observations are required to explore this possibility.

In the context of ultra-relativistic heavy ion collisions, a highly energetic parton is believed to be a significant source of heavy ion detectable signals. The energy loss this fast parton undergoes in a medium is a key concern for physicists. A newly proposed "pointing energy loss" theory is based on the fact that the energy radiated by the fast parton can be directly correlated to the location where it occurs, thus allowing for the first time, energy loss rate measurements using observables like jet quenching parameters. A comprehensive analysis of the pointing energy loss in a finite medium, considering the medium's boundaries, has been conducted in this study. The results show that in both a medium made of quarks and one consisting of gluons, the energy loss at the beginning of energy radiation is concentrated around the parton emission angle, thus being an anisotropic function. The energy loss rate is also found to be higher in the gluon medium compared to the quark medium. The study further explores the implications of this new mechanism on the energy loss of energetic partons in the initial stages of their movement, and it is observed that the newly proposed mechanism can significantly contribute to the energy loss, especially in the early phase.

In the realm of data science, the assumption of equal sample distribution is frequently overlooked, despite being a fundamental requirement for many machine learning algorithms. We address this gap by developing a new approach to statistical closest neighbor classification, which is not limited to balanced datasets. Leveraging the local linearity of a function, we establish a direct link between the distance metric and the probability density function, thereby proving that the proposed algorithm can be viewed as a form of weighted nearest neighbor classification. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method converges to a Bayesian classifier as the amount of data increases, achieving comparable performance to the more conventional closest neighbor algorithm while being applicable to real-world, unevenly distributed datasets.

We have identified 13 new, bright quasars from the SkyMapper survey, bringing the total count of known, extremely luminous quasars at redshifts greater than 3 to 21. These 21 quasars span a redshift range from 2.93 to 5.73, with 10 of them detected through the Lyman-alpha forest. Our comprehensive study of these quasars, including their spectra, luminosity functions, and accretion properties, reveals that the most luminous quasars exhibit a slight preference for odd redshift values, contradicting previous findings. Furthermore, our analysis of the quasar population at redshifts greater than 3 indicates that the distribution of their luminosity is best described by a combination of a power law and an exponential decay, rather than a pure power law, and reveals the presence of an abrupt decline in quasar luminosity at approximately 10 to 12 billion luminosity units, occurring at redshifts greater than 3.

To study the charge-tunneling process between a quantum dot and a superconducting island, we utilize a detection method based on a gate that is sensitive to electrostatic forces. This method enables the monitoring of the superconducting island's excess charge, which is not achievable through traditional transport measurements. Our results demonstrate a significant correlation between the dot's ground state and the measured charge on the island, indicating that Andreev tunneling is the dominant mechanism responsible for charge exchange. Furthermore, we found that the tunneling rate of low-energy excitations is negligible, resulting in a minimal effect of the dot's occupied Andreev bound states on the island's charge. Our findings also suggest that the dependence of tunneling rates on gate voltages is primarily influenced by the spatial localization of the tunneling sites, which can be manipulated by adjusting the gate voltages.

We develop a contraction principle for the entropic discontinuities of preservation law systems by introducing a new, more adaptable potential function that can be tailored to each equation. This enables us to derive more precise estimates, which we utilize to gain better control over potential Varschavsky type errors when solving preservation laws numerically using upwind finite volume schemes.

Current single-view 3D model generation methods are plagued by significant flaws,
such as missing or distorted details. We introduce a novel approach called
DiffDreamer, which enhances the reliability of 360-degree model creation by
leveraging a dynamic, multi-scale view management system. This system optimizes
a relevant camera position and utilizes an advanced diffusion model to produce a
high-quality, detailed texture. To ensure consistency across various views, we
integrate a conjoined latent code generated from multiple images into the diffusion
process. To address the limitations of incomplete 360-degree coverage, we apply
a novel multi-scale sampling strategy that combines image restoration with an
incomplete view completion module. Experimental results showcase the superior
performance of DiffDreamer in terms of visual quality and view coverage compared
to other leading methods.

This paper presents an evidence-based approach to predicting, improving and managing dynamic systems represented by networks and subject to stochastic changes. Focusing on systems that can be described by networks of differential equations influenced by data-driven parameters, our method relies solely on time-series information from these networks. The approach involves a statistical model for forecasting future system behavior and an optimal control technique to define the best control measures for a specified period. To validate our findings, we conducted numerical experiments on a system that incorporates an SIS epidemic model and an optimal control problem to mitigate the spread of diseases. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and its potential for practical applications.

This research is centered on the Hunter-Saxton formula, which is a hyperbolic partial differential equation, and its unique characteristic of developing singularities in finite time. We aim to establish the model's Lipschitz stability under specific conditions. By applying techniques from functional analysis, particularly weak-* topologies, we are able to derive this stability without considering the singular behavior of solutions. Additionally, we demonstrate how to circumvent this singular behavior using a new method, which we believe has significant implications for studying the stability of other hyperbolic partial differential equations with similar properties.

Assessing scoliosis using ultrasound is an effective approach as it enables early detection and monitoring. Although manual assessment is typically conducted by medical professionals, the process is susceptible to human error, potentially affecting the reliability of the analysis. To mitigate this issue, the dependence of the BI-SPINE system on scoliosis curvature is being examined to determine its potential for standardizing scoliosis evaluation and minimizing operator error. This study examines a subset of patients with scoliosis curvature ranging from 5 to 25 degrees, analyzing how the system responds to varying curvature. The research reveals that the BI-SPINE system is more reliable than human operators for scoliosis measurement and that system accuracy improves with increased curvature, although human accuracy generally improves with curvature up to a certain point before declining.

This paper introduces an innovative approach to modifying the duration of pre-existing speech segments for tasks such as speech synthesis and modification. Traditional techniques typically rely on statistical models to adjust the time span of a segment, but these models have several limitations, including the need for substantial amounts of training data. In contrast, the proposed non-statistical method is grounded in a segment's acoustic characteristics rather than derived features, making it more adaptable to various types of speech. Additionally, the new algorithm is straightforward to implement and does not require extensive computational resources. The paper showcases its effectiveness in accurately determining the time span of modified segments and provides examples of its application to tasks such as speech synthesis and modification.

Hate speech is a particularly insidious form of malicious online communication.
The inherent ambiguity of natural language poses significant challenges to hate speech detection.
To address this issue, this paper presents a novel extraction-based framework for identifying toxic characteristics in online text and utilizes this information for hate speech detection.
Our method employs an innovative approach, combining a feed-forward neural network with the long short-term memory mechanism, to automatically identify key features from a character-level representation of online text.
Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework, showcasing superior performance compared to state-of-the-art hate speech detection models.

This research paper outlines our ongoing development of an innovative approach to Multi-User MIMO communication systems, which involves the implementation of deep learning-based feature extraction and exchange techniques. Initially, each transmitter and user extracts high-level features from received signals using deep learning networks, which are then classified to determine user identity. The extracted features are transmitted over the air interface to the base station, where they are used to infer active users and estimate their channel states. Our experimental findings demonstrate that the proposed feature extraction and exchange scheme can significantly decrease the amount of data required for Multi-User MIMO processing, including channel state information overhead.

Historical manuscripts hold significant cultural and historical value, but their preservation is a pressing concern. Many of these documents are fragile and deteriorating, rendering them inaccessible to researchers. Fortunately, advancements in digital imaging and online platforms have facilitated the creation of digital archives, providing both local and global scholars with unprecedented access to these resources. A thorough examination of historical manuscript collections has been conducted, encompassing approximately 1,500 collections, both in the West and non-Western regions. These collections span from medieval to contemporary times, offering insights into the scope and diversity of available digital resources.

Robot joints' performance is severely hindered by the presence of flat surfaces, 
resulting in significant losses of precision and efficiency. To mitigate this issue, 
a novel approach has been developed, incorporating an extra sensing mechanism to 
aid the control system in detecting and minimizing the impact of flatness. The 
efficacy of this strategy was tested on an industrial robot joint, specifically the 
ABB IRB 1200, by introducing a force sensor to gauge the direction of contact and 
using a dynamic model to adjust for variations in geometry. The outcome of this 
experiment demonstrated a substantial reduction in positioning errors, 
ranging from 15% to 70%, across different scenarios.

A new method for tracking patient health over time is introduced, allowing the examination of multiple, distinct health states and their transitions. This approach is utilized to analyze the intricate relationships between various conditions and their potential pathways in patients who have experienced a myocardial infarction.

To simulate electrostatic potentials and energies of electron orbitals, the molecular continuum is typically approximated using a spherical boundary condition at a single, high boundary where the grid becomes exponentially finer. A grid design proposed in this study separates the boundary conditions into multiple spheres of varying radii for different grid points, significantly improving efficiency, particularly when the boundary conditions are solved using an iterative approach. By demonstrating the benefits of this grid design, the researchers successfully applied it to calculate the electrostatic potential of an anionic electron in multi-site configurations, including the $\mathrm{Cl}^-$ and $\mathrm{I}^-$ ions.

In the unit disk graph G, each vertex represents a disk with a fixed radius that overlaps with others when they intersect. The intersection graph resulting from these disks' non-trivial overlaps is the representation of G. The problem of finding a minimum size subset S of G's vertices that can uniquely identify all other vertices in G, known as the metric dimension problem, has been the focus of research. This specific problem has been shown to be solvable in polynomial time for chordal graphs and graphs of bounded feedback vertex group, and also for proper interval graphs of bounded clique width.

Geometric power frameworks, or directed regions, are used to model non-convex shapes in topology and have been applied in research on directed non-convexity exceptions and intersection detection. This paper defines a power structure for directed areas, allowing an extended power topology to be applied to topological spaces, and yielding various properties for directed regions in both simple and topological spaces. It also provides a characterization for the directedness of a region, along with a lemma for calculating the power structure of directed regions through induction.
